scope: Project discussion from the request for unstructured discussion through the request for documentation and layer scaffolding.
provenance: Exact message text extracted from the active conversation; only user messages and final assistant replies are included.
status: Historical source: claims in the supplied prior LLM transcript and proposals in assistant replies are not independently verified facts.

messages.text: Ok, I have an idea for a new project - in this cli directory - and I want to spend some time just having an unstructured discussion before we write any code

Let’s talk it through and let the direction emerge from the discussion. Rough thoughts, examples, and half-formed ideas are all useful.

What’s the idea, and what got you thinking about it?

My read is that **the CLI itself becomes something you describe and load**. Each project supplies its vocabulary, structure, rules, and behavior; the common runtime makes that description usable.

The JSON authoring idea gives this a concrete starting point. You can navigate a document, change things in context, inspect the differences, and accept or discard them. That is an understandable experience with a visible result.

I would keep one conclusion from the transcript open: **whether JSON authoring is the foundation of the universal CLI, or its first application**. Editing a document fits candidate state and commit naturally. An operation like “restart this service” or “follow these logs” has different expectations. Those could share navigation and discovery without every interaction becoming a document edit.

What interests me most is what “context aware” could mean beyond remembering your current path. The tool could explain what exists at that location, what you can add, which values are allowed, and which actions are available. My hypothesis is that this discoverability could be valuable to both humans and agents.

When you say “self configured,” what do you imagine giving the tool so that it becomes a CLI for a particular project?

I guess I just meant "configurable" - via some data, that could be loaded into the kernel and executed - and the resulting interface, surface and interaction is entirely derived from that configuration. I like the idea of a "layered" approach - authoring JSON itself via a contextually aware CLI becomes inherently valuable for agentic use. The VISION here for the entire project is to produce a tool that can become any CLI ever needed, and all future engineering projects stop creating manual CLIs from scratch and merely "configure or assemble" them

That clarifies the vision: **a project’s CLI becomes a loadable, composable definition, and the kernel derives the interaction from it.** Building a CLI becomes describing and assembling an interface.

The word **“entirely”** carries a lot of meaning here. Commands, navigation, argument handling, completion, validation, and help should all follow from that definition. If projects must implement those separately, we have left much of the repeated work in place.

The layered approach gives JSON authoring a useful role within that vision. It could be independently valuable while exercising the capabilities that richer interfaces would depend on: navigating context, discovering available choices, changing structured state, and inspecting results. For agents, my hypothesis is that explicitly discoverable operations and constraints would be a major part of its value.

There is also an interesting possibility: **the tool could help author the definitions that configure the tool.** If those definitions use JSON, a person or agent could construct a new CLI through the same contextual editing experience, then load it and interact with the resulting interface.

One distinction seems useful to explore: a project supplies its actual capabilities, while the kernel supplies the machinery for interacting with them. “Assemble” could therefore include reusable behavior alongside interface definitions.

Do you imagine those reusable pieces being shared across projects, so that someone could assemble a CLI partly from components other people have already defined?

Yes - the reason I bring up JSON authoring alongside the configurable CLI tool is that I believe one could help the other - CLI to configure the CLI - this could essentially close the loop on the composition such that an Agent or LLM can construct its own CLI without ever manually editing a line of JSON.

That would give the two ideas a concrete relationship: **CLI definitions become something the CLI itself knows how to author.**

An agent could enter an authoring context, discover the available building blocks, assemble an interface, validate it, and load the result. JSON would be the artifact those operations produce. The resulting definition could then be reused, shared, or opened for further editing.

There is a subtle requirement here: **context awareness must include what *could* exist, alongside what already exists.** An empty document has no keys to complete. To help an agent construct a CLI from scratch, the authoring interface would need to explain which structures it can create, what they mean, how they connect, and what remains incomplete.

That makes the description of a valid CLI particularly interesting. It could guide the construction process as well as check the finished definition. The agent would still decide what interface serves its task; the tool would help it express that decision through valid operations.

I would also distinguish successful construction from useful behavior. Loading a valid definition proves one thing; having the agent exercise the resulting CLI against its intended task would test the other. That could extend your composition loop into a **construct, use, inspect, refine** loop.

Yep. And on the authoring side - if could be used to construct literal JSON Schema objects from scratch, without ever touching a brace or bracket, or even construct an entire OpenAPI spec. Then, perhaps as a sovereign decoupled layer or "mode" this could be switched to "use the schema as a constraint system" - and then authoring becomes constrained to what the spec allows you to do. Another use for this tool is actually mocking up an entire CLI before ever attaching hooks or real functionality to any of the verbs - this then becomes a Spec Driven workflow in its own write - giving the agent a view of what functionality needs to exist in the system.

I see an important distinction here: **the document being authored and the document governing the authoring can be separate things.**

While constructing a JSON Schema, that schema is the data you are editing. A meta-schema can check its structure; once finished, your schema can constrain the construction of other documents. JSON Schema explicitly supports schemas that describe other schemas, so there is an existing foundation for that loop. [JSON Schema documentation](https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/reference/schema)

The same idea could extend to authoring an OpenAPI description, then using that description to expose operations and guide the construction of their inputs. **Authoring a specification and activating its meaning are distinct capabilities**, which fits the independence you are considering.

The mock CLI introduces another useful possibility: **people and agents could explore a proposed system through its intended interface before implementation exists.** They could discover commands, supply arguments, navigate contexts, and encounter declared responses. Trying a realistic workflow might reveal a missing operation or an awkward interaction while changing the specification is still cheap.

For that to guide implementation well, the definition would benefit from carrying expected outcomes and failure cases alongside command names and arguments. Those expectations could later become checks against the real functionality as it is attached. The mock would let you assess the interaction; those later checks would assess whether the implementation fulfills it.

There is also room for unfinished work throughout this: an agent should be able to assemble an incomplete specification and discover what remains missing before it is ready to use.

What would you want the mocked CLI to do when an agent invokes a verb whose functionality has not been implemented yet?

I think we have specified enough of this project so far to deduce how it might become valuable for agentic use. Now - I want to turn it to you: How would you use it, and what do you need it to become, and how do you need to behave - to reach the aymptote of perfection against the value it claims?

**I would use it to turn an engineering intention into an interface I can inspect, exercise, and progressively connect to real behavior.** I would want it to carry the mechanical rules of the work, leaving me to reason about purpose, meaning, and tradeoffs.

These are my requirements as a prospective user. The benefits would still need measurement.

For example, if you asked me to build a job service, I could author its job schema, construct example jobs, assemble commands for submission, inspection, and cancellation, and exercise those interactions against a mock. That experience could expose missing operations or ambiguous outcomes. As implementation arrived, I could exercise the real capabilities against the declared expectations. Another agent could load the resulting artifacts and continue the work.

The valuable output would include the interface, its constraints, and the evidence accumulated through using it.

For that to work well, I would need several things from the tool:

- **Discoverable meaning.** I need to learn what operations exist, what their inputs mean, what conditions apply, and what outcomes they promise. Completion supplies possible words; I also need enough explanation to choose the right operation.

- **Inspectable context.** I need to know which document, definition, revision, and location I am acting on; what changes are pending; and whether an operation is declared, mocked, connected, or verified. Those distinctions need to survive saving, restarting, and handing work over.

- **Precise editing with room for drafts.** Changing one field must preserve unrelated content and exact value types. I need to assemble incomplete documents, inspect unmet constraints, and receive errors that identify the affected location and rule. The tool must make its supported constraints explicit.

- **Efficient machine interaction.** I need callable operations, structured results, direct addressing, and batches where appropriate. Human interaction and agent interaction should derive their meaning from the same definitions. That is where your [verbs-as-data pattern](https://github.com/apnex/mission-kit/blob/main/patterns/P5-verbs-as-data-surface.md) becomes particularly valuable.

- **Recoverable execution.** After an interruption, I need to determine what happened before continuing. Conflicting edits, partial effects, and uncertain outcomes must be observable. A local document transaction and an external operation can offer different guarantees; the tool must describe those guarantees accurately.

- **Composition that preserves understanding.** Reusable components need discoverable requirements, effects, and compatibility rules. I should be able to understand an assembled interface through its declarations without reconstructing the internals of every component.

There is an economic requirement underneath all of this: **constructing an interface must earn back its construction cost.** For a small, isolated edit, creating a new CLI could be unnecessary work. I would expect reuse to matter greatly: learn the interaction conventions once, reuse existing definitions, and add only what the task requires. Moving the equivalent of a handwritten CLI into a configuration file would leave the original problem largely intact.

My behavior would matter just as much as the tool’s capabilities.

**I would need to stop guessing things the tool can tell me.** I should discover operations before invoking them, inspect relevant constraints, and refresh state when it changes. I should express repetitive transformations once and let deterministic machinery execute them. That is the practical value I see in your [cognitive minimalism principle](https://github.com/apnex/mission-kit/blob/main/axioms/A11-cognitive-minimalism.md).

**I would need to preserve the distinction between your intent and my interpretation.** If I author a schema, a mock, and a CLI, their agreement establishes consistency among things I created. It does not establish that I understood your request correctly. I must keep the original requirements available and test outcomes against them. Weakening a constraint simply to make my work pass would undermine the entire loop.

**I would need to verify consequences.** A successful invocation tells me something about execution. I still need evidence that the intended state or behavior resulted. Mock responses, validation results, and observations of real functionality each support different claims.

**I would need to make my work portable.** Decisions that later work depends on must live in inspectable artifacts. Another agent should be able to recover the necessary context without inheriting my private assumptions or requiring you to reconstruct the conversation.

To approach the value you claim, I would test the complete workflow against credible alternatives: targeted document edits, small scripts, and existing CLI construction methods. I would count construction effort, total tokens, elapsed time, repair attempts, human interventions, unintended changes, and independently verified task completion. Avoiding braces alone would not establish an advantage.

I would also deliberately test unfamiliar domains, malformed inputs, interrupted sessions, evolving definitions, and partially implemented systems. The “universal” claim gains substance when new kinds of CLI require less bespoke interface work while retaining their intended behavior.

**The asymptote I would aim for is that my remaining effort concerns your intent and the domain, while settled mechanical rules are reliably carried by the tool.**

A demanding demonstration would be a fresh agent loading the original requirements and saved artifacts, discovering the interface, completing an unforeseen extension, and independently verifying the result. That would test whether the understanding we built had actually become usable outside the conversation that produced it.

Reuse would matter greatly. I'm actually not too concerned about moving handwritten CLI into config all that much - though we should optimise this - the actual benefit is in the workflow to construct that configuration - i.e its no longer hand written, its progressively constructed in context - I can even see a case such that the value of the workflow outweighs the volume of the specification, such that it becomes portable and deterministic. Another thought I have is that the CLI then itself becomes a definition for another agent to resume from - a kind of structured graph that resembles the target system - that can easily be reasoned from without starting from scratch. I agree with all of the things you have listed above as valueable. Its time we begin documenting our approach to this project, a VISION, and begin scaffolding the layers
